new_statements.quote: In the rapid flow of conversation some syllables are strongly accentuated whilst others are slurred over. Consequently it is often difficult to discover the value of the unaccented vowels, and especially of the final vowel with which each word ends.
new_statements.citation: Jenness, Diamond & Andrew Ballantyne. 1920. The northern D'Entrecasteaux. Oxford: Clarendon Press. Chapter 'Language and means of communication'.

new_statements.rule_in_words: No rule is given. The source only records that Bwaidogan has prominent (accented) syllables alongside reduced unaccented ones, and that the word-final vowel is often reduced. Where the accent falls (penult, initial, etc.) is not stated anywhere in the sources that could be opened.
new_statements.exceptions: None; the source notes only that unaccented vowels, especially the final vowel of each word, are hard to hear.
new_statements.domain_note: Remark is about connected speech ('the rapid flow of conversation'), not citation forms; ethnographic language chapter, not a phonology. Lithgow 1976:475 adds only cluster-level remarks (stress phonemic in Kilivila/Muyuw/Budibud/Misima; predictable within kinship nouns and verbs across the Papuan Tip Cluster) without naming Bwaidoka. Wikipedia (from Gibson 1992 OPD) confirms stressed vs unstressed syllables condition allophony but gives no position.
new_statements.identity_note: All opened material concerns the Bwaidoka (Bwaidoga) dialect of the southeast corner of Goodenough Island (Young 1979:vi; Jenness & Ballantyne worked at Bwaidoga/Mud Bay). Jenness & Ballantyne 1920 call the language 'Bwaidogan' and contrast it with Wagifa, Belebele, Kwaiboga and Kukuya varieties; Lithgow 1976 groups Bwaidoka with Diodio, Kalokalo, Yamalele, Fagululu in the 'Bwaidoka family'. Ross 1988 tags some 'Bwaidoga (Iduna)' data, i.e. the Vivigani/Iduna variety (idun1242), distinct from Bwaidoka proper. No dialect-level glottocode issue for the 1920 quote.

sources.note: p. 57: 'In the rapid flow of conversation some syllables are strongly accentuated whilst others are slurred over. Consequently it is often difficult to discover the value of the unaccented vowels, and especially of the final vowel with which each word ends.' Establishes that syllable accent exists and that unaccented (esp. final) vowels reduce, but gives NO rule for where the accent falls.

sources.citation: Lithgow, David R. 1976. Austronesian languages: Milne Bay and adjacent islands (Milne Bay Province). In S. A. Wurm (ed.), New Guinea area languages and language study, vol. 2, 441-523. Pacific Linguistics C-39.
sources.note: Section 84 'Stress', p. 475, is a survey remark on the Papuan Tip Cluster as a whole: 'Stress is phonemic in Kilivila, Muyuw, Budibud, Misima, and probably also in Nimowa and Sud-Est. Stress is not indicated in any practical orthography. In all of the languages of PTC it seems that stress is predictable within certain word-classes, notably kinship nouns and verbs.' Bwaidoka is not named in the stress section; no Bwaidoka-specific statement.
